references_named: Tate acquisition / 'pile of bricks' press scandal (1972/1976)
rationale: A clean digital readymade of Andre's Equivalents that earns its P1: the brick count is hard-coded and invariant, so the mechanism literally cannot produce a 'richer' arrangement — equivalence is enforced, not described. Double-coding is strong (surface: tidy grid that reshuffles; depth: the Tate scandal and the readymade's value question), and the dry running counter ('rearranged N times. still 120 bricks. still equivalent.') carries the wit. Sits squarely on the chance/order axis and answers the Koons slot machine as the closest sibling in the P6 market-critique lineage.
reservations: Novelty is moderate: the mechanism (click to re-grid) is web-native but not ontologically radical — it doesn't push into territory the catalogue hasn't already mapped (cf. Mondrian favicon, Zone de Sensibilité receipt). The resize handler duplicates the render logic, which is a minor craft smell. The work is somewhat safe — it illustrates Andre's point rather than surprising the viewer with a new one.
revision_suggestion: Push the equivalence past description into structural surprise: animate the bricks physically migrating from one footprint to the next so the rearrangement itself becomes the artwork, or make the total area visibly constant across all eight layouts (e.g., a faint outline of the bounding box that persists through reshuffles). Either move would lift novelty from solid to strong without breaking the minimal gesture.
